Q23356.summary: At the top of the central leaf Christ sits enthroned, flanked by the Virgin and John the Baptist who turn toward him in intercession, the classic Byzantine Deësis; above, two angels in wreathed medallions look down. Beneath them stand five apostles with Peter at the centre, and the wings are filled with soldier saints, bishops and martyrs, each named by a carved inscription. Exquisitely refined and still bearing traces of colour, the triptych shows the court art of Constantinople at its height.
facts: It is considered the finest and best preserved of the 'Romanos group' of ivories, from a Constantinopolitan workshop probably closely tied to the imperial court.
Its name comes from its first known owner, the antiquarian Louis-François Harbaville (1791–1866) of Arras; the Louvre bought it in 1891.
According to the Louvre, the back bears the inscription IC XC NIKA ('Jesus Christ conquers'), and every figure except the two angels is identified by name.
Q23356.notes: Inv. OA 3247. The Louvre dates it 940–960 on style.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-96-christ.summary: In a cloudy heaven the nimbed Christ-Logos with a cross-staff sits in a globe-mandorla beside a personification of Justice holding scales, adored by angels — 'worship him, all ye gods'. The psalmist stands with outstretched hands on a hillock below, and all the mountains smoke, melting 'like wax at the presence of the Lord'. It is the upper of two drawings on folio 56v.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-96-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-134-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a book and raising his hand, sits on a globe supported by two personified winds — 'he bringeth the wind out of his treasuries' — among angels, on a hill in the midst of the walled city of Sion. Below, men with harps and a lute stand by the tabernacle, land is measured out 'for an heritage', and angels hurl firebrands at the first-born of Egypt. From the sun and moon tridents strike at the idols of the heathen.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-134-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-noli-me-tanger.summary: Above, two angels sit in the empty tomb beside the folded grave cloths while Christ turns to Mary Magdalene, who reaches toward him: 'touch me not'. Below, the risen Christ stands among the apostles and shows his wounded side to Thomas, who comes forward to touch it. Both scenes are set against a soft violet sky.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-noli-me-tanger.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 505); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-san-vitale-arch-christ-me.summary: At the crown of the great arch before the presbytery, a bearded Christ with long dark hair looks out from a gold-rimmed medallion, holding a book, flanked by medallions of the apostles. Set within a band of twining ornament, he presides over the chain of saints that runs down both sides of the arch. The mature, bearded type seen here contrasts with the youthful Christ enthroned on the globe in the apse just beyond.
facts: The intrados of the triumphal arch carries fifteen medallions: Christ, the Twelve Apostles and Saints Gervasius and Protasius, traditionally the sons of Saint Vitalis.
The decoration of San Vitale was begun under Bishop Ecclesius (c. 525) and the church was consecrated in 547 or 548 under Bishop Maximian.

vam:O117945.summary: Before a cave cut into a towering rock, Christ's disciples lower his body, wrapped in a shroud, into a stone sarcophagus, while in front the Virgin sinks down among the grieving holy women and other mourners stand apart at the right. On the hill at the right rise the three crosses of Calvary, and three birds fly across the wide sky that gives the print its name. The engraving's sharp parallel hatching and monumental, sculptural figures belong to the circle of Andrea Mantegna, the great Paduan master.
facts: The V&A record notes that Bartsch called this composition a copy by Giovanni Antonio da Brescia, but the cataloguer judged this impression the finer work and by Mantegna; the museum's brief description now says 'School of Andrea Mantegna', about 1500.
A painted Italian maiolica panel dated 1523, from the Salting Bequest (V&A C.2119-1910), is based on the composition of this print.
The V&A owns another impression from the Ionides Bequest (CAI.604); this one was bequeathed by the Rev. Alexander Dyce.
vam:O117945.notes: Worklist year (900) was an error: this is a late 15th-century engraving. Attribution between Mantegna and his school (or Giovanni Antonio da Brescia) is disputed. The other V&A impression (CAI.604) is in the collection separately as vam:O723054 — a different sheet, not a duplicate.

walters:W.185.49V.summary: Christ, crowned with thorns and with his wrists bound by a cord, is pushed forward by two rough tormentors toward Pilate, who sits on a wooden throne in red robes and turban, washing his hands in a golden basin with averted eyes. Christ's pale, lilac robe and lowered gaze set him apart from the vigorous figures around him. The gold ground and chequered floor are typical of the International Gothic style of the early 15th-century Netherlands.
facts: The miniature introduces Prime in the Hours of the Virgin, part of a Passion cycle of full-page miniatures marking the canonical hours (fols. 49v–91v).

The Doffinnes Hours was made in Utrecht in the first quarter of the 15th century; its twelve full-page miniatures are by the Master of Walters 185, and its pen-decorated 'G' descenders are attributed to the scribe Johannes de Malborch.
The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century and whose family recorded notes in it.
walters:W.185.49V.notes: Worklist year 750 was a parsing error for '1st quarter 15th century'. Johannes de Malborch is the scribe, not the painter.
